vignette:
At 26, she is in the middle of graduate school, the kind of student who used to measure her life in deadlines, highlighted articles, and the comfort of long evenings in the library. Before the exposure, she thinks of herself as steady and capable. She is single, close to her family, and proud of having left home to study. She talks about school as both pressure and purpose. She likes routines: coffee before class, a certain seat near the window, late-night calls with her mother in Spanish when she walks back from campus.

The event happens during a temporary research assistantship in a university laboratory. She is not reckless; if anything, she is careful, eager to do things correctly. That morning feels ordinary until it suddenly doesn’t. There is a sharp smell she cannot place at first, something metallic and burning. Then people start shouting. A container has been mishandled, and within seconds the air changes. She remembers her throat tightening before she fully understands why. Her eyes sting so badly she cannot keep them open. She hears someone say to get out, but the room is already disorienting, too bright and blurred. She coughs hard enough to vomit. On the way toward the exit, her chest feels squeezed shut, and for a moment she is certain she is going to die on that laboratory floor.

In the emergency department she is frightened and embarrassed at once, apologizing between coughs, asking questions no one answers clearly enough to satisfy her. She keeps replaying what happened, trying to decide whether she missed a warning sign or made some mistake herself. In the days afterward, she tells herself she is lucky. She was discharged. Other people were discharged too. Everyone says it could have been worse. She repeats that phrase to herself as if gratitude should cancel what her body is doing.

Instead, her body begins reacting to the world as though the exposure is still happening. Any strong odor—a bottle of bleach opened in a dorm bathroom, acetone from a nail salon, gasoline near a campus shuttle—makes her freeze. Her heart races before she can think. Her throat feels narrow. Sometimes she starts coughing just from the memory of the smell. In class, if someone uses a strong perfume, she loses track of the lecture and scans the room for exits. She starts sitting near the door and carrying a water bottle everywhere, taking small sips to reassure herself she can still swallow.

At night she dreams of air she cannot breathe. In some dreams she is back in the lab, trying to shout while no sound comes out. In others she is wandering campus and an invisible gas is spreading behind her. She wakes suddenly, sitting upright, chest pounding, her T-shirt damp with sweat. Then she lies still, listening to the radiator, the hallway, her own breathing, checking whether it is normal. Sleep becomes something she negotiates with rather than falls into. By morning she is exhausted and brittle, then ashamed of how easily she startles.

School, once organizing and familiar, becomes another place where danger seems hidden in ordinary things. She has trouble reading dense articles because the same paragraph slips past her again and again. During exams she feels detached, as if the room has gone far away. When professors mention lab work or chemical processes, she feels a jolt through her stomach. She drops opportunities that would require returning to a laboratory setting and tells people she is “too busy” or “focusing on other interests.” The explanation is easier than admitting that even walking past the science building makes her palms sweat.

She avoids talking to her family in detail because she hears the worry in her mother’s voice and does not want to become the fragile daughter everyone monitors. Still, when she is alone, she sometimes calls home just to hear ordinary kitchen sounds in the background. She misses feeling like herself with other people. Friends invite her out, but she often declines if she doesn’t know where they are going. Restaurants with cleaning chemicals in the bathroom, crowded buses, art studios with solvents—each outing requires calculations that leave her drained. She has become watchful, quick to notice vents, alarms, industrial smells, janitorial carts.

She is frustrated by how irrational this all seems to her on good days. Part of her knows she is no longer in that lab. Another part remains unconvinced. She moves through campus with the constant sense that catastrophe can come from something colorless, odorless, and overlooked. She keeps windows open even when it is cold. She reads labels obsessively. She has begun to distrust her own body, especially her breathing, monitoring it as if vigilance might prevent another collapse.

When she talks about the exposure now, she does so in a controlled voice at first, but the fear comes through in the details she cannot stop remembering: the smell, the sting in her eyes, the sound of coughing, the certainty that there would not be enough air. What troubles her most is not only that she thought she was dying, but that since then some part of her continues to live as though she still might.
